title: Transition should extend learning, not restart it
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt argues that primary to secondary transition is usually planned around visits, induction days and pastoral reassurance, while the more important question of what happens to pupils' learning gets far less attention. Pupils reach Year 7 with years of knowledge and vocabulary, yet secondary curricula often quietly ask them to begin again. She recommends that secondary colleagues look closely at Year 6 work and hold structured, subject-specific conversations with primary partners, because a general handover meeting cannot show which places, texts or concepts pupils have actually met. Revisiting familiar content is fine when it deepens understanding, but repeating a basic introduction tells pupils that their earlier learning counted for little. She acknowledges that many secondary schools take pupils from numerous primaries and that taught and securely understood are not the same, so assessment data should inform judgement rather than cap expectations. She closes with four questions leaders can use to focus a first conversation, starting small with one subject and one partner school.
points: Transition planning that stops at pastoral arrangements misses the learning side, so secondary teachers should study what Year 6 pupils are really reading, writing and reasoning about.
Subject-specific conversations with primary colleagues, built around curriculum plans and pupils' work, reveal far more than a generic handover meeting.
Revisiting prior content is valuable only when it deepens thinking, whereas re-teaching an introduction as if pupils had never met the topic devalues what they already know.
Assessment information should shape professional judgement rather than place a ceiling on what pupils are offered.
Four questions (what to preserve, build on, deepen, and where pupils are made to restart needlessly) give leaders a manageable starting point.
quotes: Pupils arrive in Year 7 with years of knowledge, vocabulary, experience and understanding behind them. Does the curriculum recognise this, or do we inadvertently ask them to begin again?

Secondary colleagues sometimes find that the work being undertaken in Year 6 is far more demanding than they had assumed. That discovery opens a productive question: if pupils have already experienced this, where should we take them next?

A general handover meeting cannot tell us everything we need to know about pupils’ learning. A conversation about geography, however, can uncover which places pupils have studied, the vocabulary they have encountered and their understanding of geographical processes. Looking together at curriculum plans and examples of work makes the discussion precise.

Familiar content provides the foundation for more sophisticated thinking. But repeating an introduction as though pupils have never encountered the subject before can leave them feeling that their earlier learning has counted for very little.

What pupils have been taught and what they securely understand will not always be identical, and both matter when deciding where to begin. Assessment information can help, but it should inform our professional judgement rather than place a ceiling on what we offer.

Leaders have an essential role here in making time for subject conversations and ensuring that what colleagues learn directly influences curriculum planning. One subject, one partnership and a few carefully chosen examples of pupils’ work can provide a manageable beginning.

Pupils should encounter new possibilities when they enter secondary school: greater depth, richer texts and more demanding questions. Most importantly, they should recognise that the learning they bring with them has somewhere to go.
